agent_notes: The text gives no date for the move. I anchor on the end of Isaac's death (Gen 35:29, where Esau and Jacob bury him together), because 36:6 reads as Esau's departure after the two brothers are again in one land, and the tradition (Rashi on 36:6) links it to Isaac's death and Jacob's return. Margin 5 years either way. Gen 32:3 already has Esau in Seir before Jacob's return, so 36:6-8 may be a retrospective summary of a move that came earlier; the reader should weigh that. If so, the event would be earlier than the one here and the margin should widen. I kept the order the chapter gives.

No journey time is computed: Canaan (Hebron) to Seir is a move of a whole household with herds and the text gives no route or duration. Duration 3 weeks is a rough estimate for a herd-bound move over about 150-290 km (Seir is 287 km from the registry's Canaan point, which is a loose centre).

Names differ from 26:34 and 28:9 (Judith/Basemath daughter of Beeri and Elon; Oholibamah daughter of Anah; Adah daughter of Elon; Basemath = Mahalath of 28:9). I did not reconcile them; the Ontologist may. 40 years +/- 3 is a loose cut because the verse gives no date.

agent_notes: A span, not a point: the sons of the three wives are born 'in the land of Canaan' (36:5). As the reviewer asked, it starts one year after the END of the Canaanite marriages and runs 40 years (the Ishmaelite marriage falls about 22 years after the start, so 20 years would have ended before Reuel), past Reuel's birth (after the Ishmaelite marriage) and before the move to Seir. The sons' order of birth is not given. Eliphaz may be born near the start of the span; Reuel certainly later.

notes.note: Verses 36:1 and 36:9-43 (generations of Esau, Horite chiefs, kings of Edom, chiefs of Edom) are left out of the events: they are undated genealogies and lists, which the skill treats as framing. 36:31 ('before any king reigned over the children of Israel') is an editorial remark, not a datable point.

No causal links are written: the reason for the move (36:7, possessions too great) is inside the event itself, and no divine or prophetic speech occurs in this chapter. A later fulfilment of Isaac's blessing of Esau (Gen 27:39-40) in the settlement of Seir could be linked by the Ontologist or a later session; I did not, because the text does not say so.
